reference.source: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours
clinicalPearls: A rare sex cord-stromal tumour that classically secretes androgens and produces virilisation in young women
Typical sequence is defeminisation (oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea and loss of female contours) followed by frank virilisation with hirsutism, deepening voice, and clitoromegaly
Usually unilateral and often diagnosed at an early stage because the hormonal effects prompt investigation
Leydig-cell differentiation may show cytoplasmic Reinke crystals, a helpful histological clue
Tumours are graded from well to poorly differentiated, and a retiform pattern or heterologous elements can be present
A subset harbour DICER1 mutations, sometimes as part of the hereditary DICER1 syndrome, so a family and personal history of related tumours is relevant
Serum testosterone is typically raised, and management is usually surgical with fertility-sparing options in young women who have early-stage disease
reference.pathophysiology: Sertoli-Leydig cell tumours are sex cord-stromal neoplasms composed of Sertoli cells, Leydig cells, and variable stroma that recapitulate testicular differentiation within the ovary. The Leydig component frequently secretes testosterone and other androgens, which suppress normal ovarian function and produce the clinical progression from defeminisation to virilisation. Histological differentiation ranges from well-formed tubules in well-differentiated tumours to poorly organised, mitotically active sheets in poorly differentiated lesions, and retiform or heterologous (for example mucinous or mesenchymal) elements may occur. Many tumours, especially those with retiform or heterologous features, carry DICER1 mutations that impair microRNA processing, linking a proportion to the inherited DICER1 tumour-predisposition syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Steroid cell tumour of the ovary
Luteoma or hyperreactio luteinalis of pregnancy
Other sex cord-stromal tumours such as granulosa cell tumour
additionalInvestigations: Serum testosterone and androgen profile to confirm hyperandrogenism
Transvaginal ultrasound to identify a solid ovarian mass
Adrenal and pelvic cross-sectional imaging to localise the androgen source
Dexamethasone suppression or related testing to distinguish adrenal from ovarian causes
Histology with immunohistochemistry (e.g. inhibin, calretinin) and DICER1 assessment where indicated
Genetic evaluation for DICER1 syndrome when clinically suggested
redFlags: Rapidly progressive virilisation in a young woman suggesting an androgen-secreting tumour
Markedly elevated serum testosterone with a solid ovarian mass
Poorly differentiated histology or heterologous elements indicating higher malignant potential
Personal or family history of DICER1-associated tumours
reference.prognosis: Well-differentiated tumours are almost always benign and cured by conservative surgery, and androgenic features often regress afterwards. Intermediate and poorly differentiated tumours carry a real risk of recurrence and malignant behaviour, so outlook depends heavily on grade and stage.
pitfalls: Attributing hyperandrogenism to polycystic ovary syndrome and missing a small androgen-secreting tumour
Failing to distinguish an ovarian from an adrenal source of androgen excess
Overlooking DICER1 syndrome and the implications for the patient and relatives
Underestimating malignant potential in poorly differentiated or retiform tumours
references: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours
Blaustein's Pathology of the Female Genital Tract
management: Fertility-sparing unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with surgical staging is the mainstay for well-differentiated, early-stage tumours in young women
Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and debulking for advanced-stage or poorly differentiated disease in those who have completed childbearing
Adjuvant platinum-based combination chemotherapy (bleomycin-etoposide-cisplatin) for poorly differentiated, ruptured, or advanced-stage tumours
Symptomatic support for hirsutism and voice change, anticipating partial regression of virilising features after resection
Surveillance with serial serum testosterone and androgen profile as a recurrence marker, alongside pelvic imaging
Germline DICER1 testing with genetic counselling and family screening for DICER1-associated tumours where a mutation is confirmed
Coordinate care through a gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary team
